Three variants of a new Ni-based superalloy (Alloy1, Alloy2, Alloy3) were designed and studied, with equal equilibrium γ' volume fraction at 900°C but varying (Nb+Ta)/Al ratios.
The new alloy variants showed no evidence of cracking in the bulk during L-PBF processing, unlike CM247LC which exhibited solid-state, solidification, and liquation cracking.
All compositions showed some gas porosity, especially at thin wall sections like the trailing edge of the turbine blade geometry.
A novel sub-solvus heat treatment (HT3) was found to be most appropriate for the new alloys, avoiding the embrittlement seen with super-solvus heat treatment (HT1).
The tensile strength of the new superalloy was greatest when the Nb+Ta content was highest (in Alloy3) and exceeded that of CM247LC up to ~900°C.
The creep resistance of CM247LC following HT3 exceeded that of the new alloy variants, likely due to CM247LC's greater γ' volume fraction and higher C and B contents.
Atom probe tomography showed the concentrations of Nb and Ta in the γ' of Alloy3 were approximately twice as high as those in Alloy1.
Micro-XCT revealed cracking throughout the top 1 mm of the CM247LC turbine blade, with the cracks appearing plate-like in the build direction and skeleton-like in the XY plane.
Oxidation resistance was best when the Al content was highest, and oxidation-assisted cracking resistance was maximized when the (Nb+Ta)/Al ratio was balanced.
Oxidation-assisted cracking testing at 800°C and various strain rates allowed for the assessment of the influence of oxidation on crack growth.
The new alloy variants were designed using the Alloys-by-Design (ABD) method, considering processability, creep resistance, oxidation resistance, strength, and density.
The powder feedstock had a median particle diameter (D50) between 32.3 and 33.0 μm, with D10 and D90 values of ~19 and 55 μm respectively.
L-PBF processing was carried out using a Renishaw AM 400 system with a 200 W pulsed fiber laser, 30 μm layer thickness, and 0.875 m/s scan speed.
Differential scanning calorimetry was used to determine the γ' solvus temperatures, which were 1172, 1179, 1182, and 1249°C for Alloy1, Alloy2, Alloy3, and CM247LC respectively.
Thermo-gravimetric analysis was used to assess the oxidation resistance of the alloys at 1000°C in laboratory air.
